utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Would the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-94-2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could someone bring the accused into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Before we start, let me say hello to everyone, welcome you here. I -- my name is Carmen Agius. I come from Malta, and I have been appointed as the Trial Judge for this case. Before I proceed, I would like a confirmation from the Defendant that he understands -- he is hearing the proceedings in a language which he understands. There is a problem with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Howard Morrison for the Defendant. I think he's just receiving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me? No. So I'll repeat the question. Mr. Nikolic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So before I proceed, I would like to know from you whether you can hear what is being said in a language that you can understand. Okay. So for your benefit, I will just repeat very briefly what I said before. I introduced myself. My name is Carmen Agius. I come from Malta, and I am the Trial Judge in this case. I also want to welcome everyone and look forward to cooperating with both the Prosecution and the Defence in this case. Can you still hear me and follow what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'd like to know now who is representing who. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honour. I'm Upawansa Yapa appearing for the Prosecution, with Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. William Smith. Mr. David Leese, is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, Howard Morrison for the Defendant. May I repeat, we are in reverse Your Honour's greeting and welcome Your Honour to The Hague and this Tribunal and hope that you have a fulfilling career here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can start. As you remember, the last Status Conference was held on the 29th of August of last year, and this Status Conference is being convened more or less in the time limit established by the Rules in order to organise exchanges between the parties and take stock of the case as it stands now, particularly in view of the latest developments, which I will be referring to very shortly, and try to organise ourselves better in preparation for the trial that will take place in due course. As you know, and perhaps I would like confirmation of this from Mr. Morrison, there has been a motion filed by the Prosecution to -- for leave to amend the first amended indictment. I was given a copy of it yesterday morning. I've gone through it. I have also more or less compared it with the first amended indictment in preparation for today's hearing. What I want to know first and foremost from you, Mr. Morrison, is whether you have received a copy and whether you've had time to go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the position is this: I had a conference with my learned friend for the Prosecution on the 21st of December last, and a draft copy of the proposed new indictment was given to me. That is substantially the same as the now-filed indictment. So I have the period between the 21st of December and now to consider the -- the practicalities of it. But, of course, until it was filed in its final form, which I received it yesterday, I haven't been able to go through it with any more determination than that. Now, it has been filed, and before I can go through it with Mr. Nikolic, it will have to be translated for him. Otherwise, I'm going to have to go through it section by section together with an interpreter, which would be a very unsatisfactory way of dealing with it. It's far better that he has a translated copy, has the opportunity to read it, and then for me to go through it once he's done that. I've told him this morning of its existence, but he knows no more about it than that. So I -- if it's necessary for Your Honour to make an indication that the Registry should now provide translation services for that indictment on the assumption that it is going to be the indictment in the case, I'd -- I'd welcome Your Honour's, as it were, intervention in that matter, because that needs to be done as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can do that undoubtedly, and I would suppose that the -- from the Prosecution side, there's no objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection, and from what I understand, it is being translated at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: So hopefully we will get a copy soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I don't even need to make an order to that because I take it that it will be ready and handed over as soon as possible. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: In which case, may I formally say, so there's no doubt, that I not only have no objection to the amended indictment, I welcome it. This is an amendment that the Defence has been pursuing for some time. And may I, without embarrassing him, congratulate Mr. Upawansa Yapa for having taken the case over relatively recently, produced it in a very short space of time, bearing in mind it's now 20 months since the Defendant was arrested and seven years since the original indictment. So I think it's a world record. I've never heard of an indictment being amended after seven years, but I'm grateful for it. As Your Honour can see, it's reduced the counts from 80 to 8, it's a much more logical, and with great respect to the original drafting, a much more logical and concise document. It's going to be much easier to work with. And so officially, I don't oppose the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend the first amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I also should like to congratulate you, Mr. Yapa, because when I first started taking cognisance of this case about a month and a half ago, one of things that was really annoying me was the fact that for months and months -- actually for over a year there had been this promise from the Prosecution to reduce the number of counts from 80-something-odd counts that it was to what it is now. So I -- I take that as a clear sign from the Prosecution that it will be cooperating as much as is needed in this case, to start and finish. It's a case that should not take longer than one would expect -- reasonably expect it to take. So having established that on the Defence side, there is no opposition for the motion of the Prosecution for leave to amend the first amended indictment, I think it's not the case of asking you, Mr. Morrison, for any further comments on the substance of the indictment, because I understood that you are reserving your position after you have consulted your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must. So if Your Honour is granting the Prosecution's leave and the first amended indictment is going to now -- the amended first amended indictment is now going to be the indictment in the case, may I then make the observation that of course under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the defendant should be rearraigned on the fresh indictment. But, of course, I would ask that that not be done today because of the factors that I've already raised. I will as soon as practicable indicate to the Court when the Defence is ready for rearraignment. But that in itself need not slow the process down. That can be done, as it were, along the way. For the moment -- for all practical purposes, if I indicate that for today's hearing, we are content to leave it at that, as far as the Defence is concerned, as far as the indictment is concerned, if the Court is content to leave it on that basis. I can't give Your Honour a time estimate, because I don't know when the translated indictment is going to be in my hands. All I can say is it will be done as soon as practicable after I have received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as far as this motion for leave to amend the first amended indictment, I will be deciding it in the course of the next few days, and in all probability within a week from today, and I will then obviously do what -- what has been mentioned, in other words, appoint another day as -- with the Rules anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And of course you will have ample time to consult your client and file any document that you deem fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I think the time scale then, is this, Your Honour, that the -- because the new indictment contains the, as it were, amended charges, there would now technically be another 30-day period starting from the day that the indictment is endorse by Your Honour, not from today, but from whatever day in the future that is going to be. We have 30 days to file any fresh Rule 72 motions. That brings me onto the existing Rule 72 motion, which is pending. Such a motion was filed on the 29th of October, last. And Your Honour will note the motion itself is not particularly voluminous, but it contains huge amounts of material. There has been a response from the Prosecution and a reply to that response, but the matter has not yet been adjudicated. Once that original, if I may put it like that, Rule 72 motion has been determined by the Trial Chamber, the question then arises as to whether or not there will be from either side any interlocutory appeal. The chances are that there would be, whatever the determination of the Trial Chamber and because it's a fundamental issue that's being raised. With the best will in the world, bearing the mind the realpolitik of the speed of the Tribunal under these matters, that isn't going to happen, I suggest, for between now and the end of February at the earliest, with everybody working as expeditiously as possible. That having been the case, there is then the question of a minimum six-week period between the filing of a Prosecution pre-trial brief and a Pre-Trial Conference. That's a minimum period. Bearing in mind the change in the indictment and the perhaps rather different angle the Defence might have to come from, and hitherto has been anticipated, it's more likely there will be another two-month delay. Well, that will take us to the end of -- from the end of February to the end of April. So for anyone who is interested in my observations, all I can say is that the assessment from the Defence side is that this is a case that if it goes to trial will be very unlikely to be ready for trial before May of this year. And that's simply following the -- the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, let alone any extraneous matters which may arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So with regard to the motion on -- that you've just referred to on the legality of the arrest, and as it affects all -- all the proceedings in terms of Rule 72, the position is as follows: The Tribunal is -- the Chamber is working on it. It's in the process of elaborating a decision. Of course I understand -- fully understand that it -- it is not affected by the fact that a motion for -- for leave to amend the bill of indictment -- the indictment has been filed. That has got absolutely nothing to do with it. So in other words, as I just wanted to inform you, that the Tribunal will in due course decide this -- this matter irrespective of the new bill of -- the new indictment and the observations and documents that have to be filed in due course with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. And Your Honour will of course be aware that the -- part of the reasoning behind the way in which the -- that motion was drafted and presented was because it was at the invitation of Judge Hunt that the issues be determined in that way, rather than go down the road that was followed in the case of Todorovic, which ended up in an extremely long and time-consuming debate that never came to a fruitful end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you will understand, Mr. Morrison, that my problem was that when I arrived here and tried to take stock of the -- of the situation, this is not the only case I'm dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I found two, three box files there with documents related only and exclusively to this motion on the legality of the arrest. And of course, with my legal stuff, I also tried to organise myself and obtain the documentation that was filed in the Todorovic case, which as you know ended up with -- with a plea bargaining or whatever, plea of guilty -- guilt anyway, and that solved the whole matter. This issue or the documentation that has been presented, both from your side and particularly from the Prosecution side, is voluminous and it is being studied, I mean, including all the copious references to orders and articles and whatever, which -- some of which are very pertinent, some of which are completely relevant, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's the nature of the beast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: One has to put in that which is germane, as well as that which may not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why it's taking time. You know, I mean, it's taking time. I can assure you that my legal staff is working very hard on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I know the time scale. I think it took me 200 hours to read all the documents myself, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is. It is voluminous. Unfortunately -- you know, I mean -- and I would have appreciated more very serious attempt at discriminating between some material and other. For example, there is a reference to a decision of the European Court of Human Rights, which I have gone through, and which I find very significant or very relevant to the -- to the particulars of this case or even the legal issues involved. And the same applies to several articles that have been filed. Anyway, but still we have to go through that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and find -- find what's relevant, what's important, and what's not. But I assure you that it's given -- being given the utmost attention, and it is my intention to reduce the time span between now and the beginning of the trial as much as I can. And I will do my best to do that. Okay? Given that, as you know, new arrangements are in place now, assuring that there will be six trials going on simultaneously, some in the morning, some in the afternoon or evening, and that has to be taken into consideration as well, because as long as these six trials are still being heard, I mean, we might as well finish all the preliminary proceedings, procedures, and we will still not be able to start the trial. But in any case, more or less things are in plan, and -- and I think as far as your client's case is concerned, the situation is pretty much in hand, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged for that observation. I wait with interest to see how everybody copes with running six trials simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's also -- when I said -- it's not just postures you want. It's also wishful thinking sometimes. But let's be pragmatic about it, and we'll see how it works. I will be starting with a trial later on this month. Hopefully, unless there would be fresh developments there, which would mean delaying it further -- and this is not a trial that is going to last a few days or a few weeks, as you know. You know, the situation is changed more or less radically now that the number of counts have been reduced to eight. When I was doing the comparative exercise between yesterday and this morning, I think the time span needed for the -- for this trial from beginning to end should be radically reduced. You know, I mean, because there are, for example, with regard to the original first amended -- to the first amended amendment -- indictment, several accusations related to several persons have now been eliminated, and that could -- I mean, I'm not in a position to confirm this, but that would presumably reduce the number of witnesses considerably. You know, I mean, I don't know. You are in a better position to make an assessment of that. And once you can give us that assessment, then obviously we can plan better. So I'm sure that that is the case. I mean, but I'm also sure that you probably know much better than I do what the situation looks like. Okay? Would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I'm thankful to Your Honour for the observations that were made and also I should thank Your Honour and my learned friend for the compliments made on the shortened indictment. As Your Honour was pleased to explain a little while ago, the number of counts have been reduced drastically, and there was good reason for us to do that. And the list of witnesses also has been shortened to a great extent. So it would mean, definitely, the time taken for the case will be shortened to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you expect it to last? A rough guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is somewhat difficult to make an assessment, but I would say for the Prosecution case, a maximum length of six weeks would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Morrison, from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that you first probably will have to see what the list of -- new list of witnesses is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's something I'm going to have to discuss, of course, with the OTP, to find out now exactly how they intend to -- I can see what the indictment is. I can guess how it's going to be prosecuted, but of course it is merely a guess at the moment. The realistic position is that this trial, if it proceeded to trial, on an eight-count indictment, I think would be completed within -- within a four-month period, probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good to know and good to hear. Okay. May I now proceed -- something else. Is there anything that you would like to raise with regard to Rule 66(A) or Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment, I do not have in respect of the Status Conference that is on at present to make any observation. But I should inform the Chamber and my learned friend that the -- the other matters relating to the trial as are required in terms of the Rules are being attended to. And it's a continuing process in respect of our obligations, we are continuing to attend to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't always happen, but I've been fortunate in this case with all counsel from the OTP, I have complete confidence that the matters which should be disclosed will be disclosed and I understand -- as Your Honour knows, in the U.K. as a barrister one Prosecutes and defends; you don't just defend. So I spend in the U.K. half my life prosecuting. I know the difficulties of prosecuting a case and organising disclosure very well. I am content, of course, to leave it in the hands of the serried ranks of the opposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before we adjourn, actually I would like to ask Mr. Nikolic whether you would like to raise any issue, any matter relating to your state of health or the condition of your detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been through these matters with my client prior to trial. The indication from him was that there was no specific matter that he wished to bring to the Court's attention, unless he's had a change of heart on that. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, if there is any reason for such complaints between now and the next Status Conference or the next hearing, whatever kind of hearing that would be, please do make sure that that complaint reaches me through your Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can leave it at that. Recapitulating, point one is the Tribunal will decide on the motion for leave to amend the first-amended indictment, taking into consideration the non-opposition on the part of the Defence as recorded in today's hearing. Secondly, that the Tribunal will in due course decide the issue, the motion on the illegality of the arrest to which the Defence made reference earlier on; and following the decision by the Tribunal with regard to the motion to amend -- for leave to amend the first-amended indictment, then obviously the Rules -- the procedure laid down in the Rules will be observed and there will be usual opportunities for the Defence to file whatever documentation needs within the time limit established in the Rules -- in the Rules. And we can leave it at that. And I adjourn the hearing. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
